title: 1 Chronicles 15:16–29
context: 1 Chronicles 15:16–29 describes the Levitical singers and musicians, the doorkeepers, and the procession that brings the ark from Obed-Edom’s house to David’s city. The parallel in 2 Samuel 6:12–16 is shorter, and the differences are named rather than harmonized: Chronicles reports that when God helped the Levites they sacrificed seven bulls and seven rams (15:26), where 2 Samuel 6:13 reports an ox and a fattened calf after six paces; and Chronicles adds a robe of fine linen as well as the linen ephod (15:27). Some musical terms here, such as Alamoth and the term rendered “the eight-stringed lyre,” are of uncertain meaning; Alamoth also appears in the heading of Psalm 46. The singer Ethan is called the son of Kushaiah here and the son of Kishi in 6:44. Chronicles records Michal’s inner contempt in a single verse and does not narrate the exchange of 2 Samuel 6:20–23. Both traditions read her soberly, within the painful history between Saul’s house and David’s, without caricature, and they share the view that this is joyful worship offered on God’s terms.

verses.text: David spoke to the chief of the Levites to appoint their brothers as singers with instruments of music, stringed instruments, harps, and cymbals, sounding aloud and lifting up their voices with joy.
verses.arminianNotes:
David tells the chief of the Levites to appoint their brothers as singers with instruments of music, stringed instruments, harps, and cymbals, lifting up their voices with joy.

Arminian readers see joy and order joined together, and they note that David wants the people’s gladness expressed through skilled and willing singers who give themselves freely to the praise of God before the whole assembly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Chronicles connects music with the ordered service of the Levites (compare 6:31–32), so that praise is not left to chance but is appointed and arranged as part of the worship God receives.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: joyful praise and careful order are not rivals in the worship of the LORD.

verses.text: So the Levites appointed Heman the son of Joel; and of his brothers, Asaph the son of Berechiah; and of the sons of Merari their brothers, Ethan the son of Kushaiah;
verses.arminianNotes:
The Levites appoint Heman son of Joel, Asaph son of Berechiah, and Ethan son of Kushaiah from the sons of Merari. In 6:44 Ethan is called the son of Kishi, and the difference is recorded rather than harmonized.

Arminian readers note that the leading singers are drawn from different Levitical families, and they see shared service across family lines as part of the people’s united response to God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the same three leaders appear in the list of singers in 6:33–44, Heman among the Kohathites, Asaph among the descendants of Gershom, and Ethan among the sons of Merari, which shows continuity in the ordering of worship.

Both traditions read the verse as a record of appointed leaders and treat it as shared ground.

verses.text: and with them their brothers of the second rank: Zechariah, Ben, Jaaziel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Unni, Eliab, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattithiah, Eliphelehu, Mikneiah, Obed-Edom, and Jeiel, the doorkeepers.
verses.arminianNotes:
With them are their brothers of the second rank, including Zechariah, Ben, Jaaziel, and others, with Obed-Edom and Jeiel as doorkeepers. The short name Ben does not reappear in the list at 15:20, and Jaaziel here appears as Aziel there.

Arminian readers see second-rank servants honored by name, a reminder that supporting roles in worship matter to God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Obed-Edom appears here as a Levitical doorkeeper, and that whether he is the same as Obed-Edom the Gittite of 13:13 is debated, so they hold the identification loosely.

Both traditions treat the small differences between the name lists as matters for study rather than doctrine, and they read the verse as shared ground about service.

verses.text: So the singers, Heman, Asaph, and Ethan, were given cymbals of bronze to sound aloud;
verses.arminianNotes:
The singers Heman, Asaph, and Ethan are given bronze cymbals to sound aloud. The leaders have the instruments that keep the rhythm and signal the music.

Arminian readers see the leading singers taking up their task with energy, and they note that God’s praise is meant to be heard, offered openly and joyfully before the whole assembly rather than kept as a private matter.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the assignment of particular instruments to particular people shows the careful ordering of Levitical worship, which Chronicles presents as part of David’s faithful arrangements for the house of God.

Both traditions read the verse as practical detail in service of joyful worship and treat it as shared ground without building doctrine on it.

verses.text: and Zechariah, Aziel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Unni, Eliab, Maaseiah, and Benaiah, with stringed instruments set to Alamoth;
verses.arminianNotes:
Zechariah, Aziel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Unni, Eliab, Maaseiah, and Benaiah play stringed instruments set to Alamoth. Alamoth is a musical term of uncertain meaning; it also appears in the heading of Psalm 46.

Arminian readers note that skill and preparation are offered to God, and they see the musicians’ willing labor as part of a wholehearted response.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers agree that the term is uncertain and avoid building interpretation on a guessed meaning, while noting that the verse shows praise arranged with care according to settled patterns of music.

Both traditions hold the musical details lightly, treat the verse as shared ground, and read it as an example of thoughtful, ordered worship offered to the LORD.

verses.text: and Mattithiah, Eliphelehu, Mikneiah, Obed-Edom, Jeiel, and Azaziah, with harps tuned to the eight-stringed lyre, to lead.
verses.arminianNotes:
Mattithiah, Eliphelehu, Mikneiah, Obed-Edom, Jeiel, and Azaziah play harps “tuned to the eight-stringed lyre,” to lead. The musical meaning of this term is uncertain.

Arminian readers see different groups of musicians each contributing their part, and they note that a variety of gifts can serve together in the praise of God when each is offered willingly and with care.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the term may refer to a musical setting or pitch, but they refrain from claiming more than can be known, and they read the verse as part of Chronicles’ detailed record of Levitical service.

Both traditions treat the musical terms as matters for study, not doctrine, and they read the verse as shared ground about the ordering of praise.

verses.text: Chenaniah, chief of the Levites, was over the singing. He taught the singers, because he was skillful.
verses.arminianNotes:
Chenaniah, chief of the Levites, is over the singing and teaches the singers because he is skillful. Some interpreters take the term rendered singing to refer instead to the carrying of the ark; the meaning is uncertain.

Arminian readers see gifts recognized and used for the good of others, as Chenaniah teaches those under him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that skill is honored as a gift fitted for service in God’s house, and they see the appointment of a capable leader as part of the proper ordering of worship, whichever task the term describes.

Both traditions read the verse as affirming that skill and teaching have a place in worship and treat it as shared ground.

verses.text: Berechiah and Elkanah were doorkeepers for the ark.
verses.arminianNotes:
Berechiah and Elkanah are doorkeepers for the ark. They guard access to the ark during the procession.

Arminian readers see that even guarding a door is a real service to God, and they note that faithfulness in modest tasks matters as much as leadership in more visible roles within the community of worship.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the appointment of doorkeepers for the ark reflects the lesson of chapter 13: the holiness of God’s presence must be guarded, and approach to it must be ordered according to his word rather than left open to careless handling.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about reverent care for the things of God.

verses.text: Shebaniah, Joshaphat, Nethanel, Amasai, Zechariah, Benaiah, and Eliezer, the priests, blew the trumpets before God’s ark; and Obed-Edom and Jehiah were doorkeepers for the ark.
verses.arminianNotes:
The priests Shebaniah, Joshaphat, Nethanel, Amasai, Zechariah, Benaiah, and Eliezer blow the trumpets before God’s ark, and Obed-Edom and Jehiah are doorkeepers for the ark. The law had said, “The sons of Aaron, the priests, shall blow the trumpets” (Numbers 10:8).

Arminian readers see the priests faithfully taking up their appointed part.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the trumpet blowing by priests follows the law’s ordinance, which again shows that the second procession is grounded in God’s word, and they see priests and Levites each serving in their own role.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about ordered worship in which every appointed servant has a place before the LORD.

verses.text: So David, the elders of Israel, and the captains over thousands went to bring the ark of the LORD’s covenant up out of the house of Obed-Edom with joy.
verses.arminianNotes:
David, the elders of Israel, and the captains over thousands go to bring the ark of the LORD’s covenant up from Obed-Edom’s house with joy. The parallel is 2 Samuel 6:12, which also says David heard that the LORD had blessed Obed-Edom’s house.

Arminian readers see the leaders choosing to go personally and gladly, and they note that joy now accompanies obedience.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the ark is now called the ark of the LORD’s covenant, which links it with the covenant God made with Israel, and they see joy returning when worship is offered according to God’s instructions.

Both traditions read the verse as the fulfillment of David’s desire to center Israel’s life on God’s presence and treat it as shared ground.

verses.text: When God helped the Levites who bore the ark of the LORD’s covenant, they sacrificed seven bulls and seven rams.
verses.arminianNotes:
When God helps the Levites who bear the ark of the LORD’s covenant, they sacrifice seven bulls and seven rams. The parallel in 2 Samuel 6:13 says that when “those who bore the LORD’s ark” had gone six paces, David sacrificed an ox and a fattened calf; the difference is noted here.

Arminian readers see God’s help enabling the Levites’ real obedience.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that Chronicles credits the success first to God’s help, so that even obedient service depends on his grace. Both affirm divine help and human action together.

Neither tradition builds a contrast on this verse; both read the sacrifices as thanksgiving and reverence, and they keep the two accounts’ different details without harmonizing them.

verses.text: David was clothed with a robe of fine linen, as were all the Levites who bore the ark, the singers, and Chenaniah the choir master with the singers; and David had an ephod of linen on him.
verses.arminianNotes:
David is clothed with a robe of fine linen, as are the Levites who bear the ark, the singers, and Chenaniah the choir master, and David also wears a linen ephod. The parallel in 2 Samuel 6:14 mentions the linen ephod and David dancing with all his might.

Arminian readers see the king dressing like those who serve, humbling himself before the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that linen was associated with priestly service (compare 1 Samuel 2:18, where the young Samuel wears a linen ephod), and that interpreters discuss what David’s wearing it meant.

Both traditions read the verse as joyful humility in worship rather than display, and they let Chronicles’ added detail stand beside Samuel’s account.

verses.text: Thus all Israel brought the ark of the LORD’s covenant up with shouting, with sound of the cornet, with trumpets, and with cymbals, sounding aloud with stringed instruments and harps.
verses.arminianNotes:
All Israel brings up the ark of the LORD’s covenant with shouting, the sound of the cornet, trumpets, cymbals, stringed instruments, and harps. The parallel in 2 Samuel 6:15 mentions shouting and the sound of the trumpet.

Arminian readers see the whole nation joining gladly in the celebration, with the joy of the first attempt now joined to obedience to God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the verse as the climax of the procession, in which the full ordered worship described in this chapter accompanies the ark to its place, and they note Chronicles’ fuller list of instruments.

Both traditions read the scene as the right fulfillment of David’s desire and as shared ground about joy and reverence together.

verses.text: As the ark of the LORD’s covenant came to David’s city, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out at the window, and saw king David dancing and playing; and she despised him in her heart.
verses.arminianNotes:
As the ark comes to David’s city, Michal the daughter of Saul looks out of the window, sees King David “dancing and playing” and despises him in her heart. The parallel in 2 Samuel 6:16 has “leaping and dancing before the LORD”

Arminian readers note that the narrator calls her the daughter of Saul, placing her response within the conflict between Saul’s house and David’s.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Chronicles records only her inner contempt and does not narrate the exchange in 2 Samuel 6:20–23, and they recognize the painful history between Michal and David (1 Samuel 18–19; 2 Samuel 3:13–16).

Both traditions read the verse soberly, without caricaturing or speculating about Michal beyond what the text says.
